title: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Hypervisor CLI
shortTitle: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Hypervisor CLI
summary: A hypervisor is the layer that runs virtual machines, and its command line offers administrative power over every guest on the host, which makes it a high value execution surface. On VMware ESXi the relevant tools are esxcli and vim-cmd, which can list registered virtual machines, power them on or off, change the host firewall, redirect log forwarding, add or modify local accounts, and enable or disable services including remote shell access. Comparable interfaces exist elsewhere, such as the Hyper-V PowerShell module on Windows or an administration console on other platforms. The abuse pattern in real intrusions combines discovery with impact: enumerate guests, force them off, delete or encrypt their disk files, then reduce the chance of being recorded by changing log forwarding or clearing shell history. Because hypervisor hosts are rarely instrumented with endpoint agents, the evidence usually lives in the host's own files and in the central log collector. ESXi writes administrative shell activity to its shell log and host daemon activity to hostd, and both flow to a remote syslog server when forwarding is configured. The discriminator is context: a vim-cmd power operation during a maintenance window from the management network is routine, while the same command issued from a new address, followed by mass power-off events and a change to syslog configuration, is an incident.

beginner.definition: A hypervisor is the software layer that runs virtual machines on a physical server. It has its own command line for administrators. This technique is about attackers using that command line to control the machines it hosts.
beginner.whyItMatters: One hypervisor command can affect every virtual machine on the host. These servers often have no security agent installed, so few alerts come from them. Attackers have used this access to switch off many machines at once and then damage their storage. If you do not collect hypervisor logs, that activity may leave no trace you can read.
howItWorks: An attacker signs in to the hypervisor console or remote shell with stolen administrator credentials.
They use built-in tools to list every virtual machine registered on the host.
They can power machines off, delete them, or act on the files behind them.
They can change host firewall rules and enable services such as remote shell access.
They often redirect or disable log forwarding so the host stops reporting to your collector.
On other platforms the same control is offered through a PowerShell module or web console.
beginner.example: Imagine a block of flats with one caretaker's cupboard in the basement. Inside that cupboard are the master switches for every flat's heating and water. The caretaker uses it daily, so nobody questions it. A stranger who gets into the cupboard can shut off every flat with three switches. He can also stop the building cameras from recording. A hypervisor command line is that cupboard, and the flats are the virtual machines.
takeaways: Treat hypervisor administrator accounts as the most sensitive accounts you hold.
Send hypervisor logs to a remote server that the host itself cannot edit.
Mass virtual machine power events are a strong sign of destructive activity.

objectives: Explain what a hypervisor is and why its command line controls many machines at once.
Describe the administrative actions an attacker can take through hypervisor tools.
Name the hypervisor log files and remote log forwarding that record this activity.
Explain how this sub-technique differs from the parent technique, Command and Scripting Interpreter.
Recognise the combination of enumeration and log tampering that marks destructive intent.
